title: Golden Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Golden wells have a 70 ft median depth, but local records range to 1,997 ft. See yields, costs, water levels and risks.
h1: Golden, Colorado Well Depth, Yield and Drilling Costs
intro_html:
Buying land or a house in Golden means looking beyond the permit label. Records within five miles show a wide range of well conditions: the median reported depth is 70 feet, while the middle half runs from 29 to 300 feet. Reported yields are generally useful, but the ground changes quickly between mountain locations, fractured bedrock and sedimentary formations.

This page uses Colorado DWR permit records for Golden and nearby areas including West Pleasant View, Applewood, East Pleasant View, Fairmount, Genesee and Idledale. Use the results to frame a site-specific drilling bid and to identify questions about water quality, septic design, access and the intended household use.

sections.heading: Golden well depths change sharply by ground
sections.html:
Golden’s reported well depth is shallow by regional standards at the median: 70 feet. The middle half of reported wells falls between 29 and 300 feet, but the 90th percentile reaches 565 feet and the deepest record is 1,997 feet. That spread matters when you price a new well. A nearby shallow completion does not guarantee the same result on a lot across a drainage or against the foothills.

About 55% of reported wells are under 100 feet. Another 19% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 16% between 300 and 600 feet, and 9% exceed 600 feet. Permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers most often, with Denver and alluvial aquifers also recorded. Fractured rock can make depth and water production difficult to predict from surface location alone.

sections.heading: Most Golden wells report a workable yield
sections.html:
Among the wells that report a pump yield, the median is 7.2 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 5.0 to 11.0 gallons per minute, which is a useful range for ordinary household planning when the well, storage system and septic design are all appropriate.

Yield is not the same as a continuous guarantee. About 64% of reported wells fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 21% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. About 3% report under 1 gallon per minute, and 12% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 503 wells report a pump yield, so ask for the original well test rather than relying only on the neighborhood median.

sections.heading: Water levels vary across Golden’s mountain ground
sections.html:
The median reported static water level is 60 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 16 to 120 feet. That range affects pump setting, trenching and the amount of lift a system must handle. It also shows why a water level from one property should not be treated as a measurement for the next lot.

The decade series does not show a simple, steady decline. Median depth to water was 26 feet in the 1960s, 92 feet in the 1980s, 21 feet in the 2010s and 120 feet in the 2020s. The records are uneven by location and measurement, with only 125 wells reporting a static water level, so this is a warning to verify current conditions rather than proof of one uniform groundwater trend.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long use and continuing activity
sections.html:
Golden has a long well history in the DWR records. Permits were issued in every decade from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the busiest period in the 1990s at 786 permits. The records include 667 permits from the 2000s, 409 from the 2010s and 196 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The database contains 4,246 wells within the study area. Of those, 2,475 are recorded as constructed. The most active driller names in the records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), James Drilling Company, and Aspen Drilling Company Inc. These names help when tracing local permit history, but a current bid still needs to account for access, casing, grout, formation and the exact proposed site.

sections.heading: A median-depth Golden well starts near the middle cost range
sections.html:
The cost model for Golden’s Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the 70-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $3,500 to $4,900. That is only the drilling portion, not a complete operating water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $9,500 to $16,900 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access route or additional casing and grouting can move the proposal beyond that range. Get the bid in writing and ask what happens if the driller reaches the planned depth without an adequate supply. Compare the water system cost with the septic and site-development work before setting a total construction budget.

sections.heading: Golden buyers need to check quality, yield and septic fit
sections.html:
Water quantity is only one part of the decision. Within about 10 miles, the mapped environmental inventory includes 170 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 200 historic mine features and 25 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped sites do not establish contamination at a particular well, but they are good reasons to review nearby land uses, test the existing well and ask what treatment may be needed.

Low-yield wells, dry holes and changing fractured-rock conditions remain practical risks. Confirm the permit’s approved use before assuming a well supports a home, irrigation or livestock. Septic setbacks, replacement-area requirements, access for drilling equipment, slope and electrical service also need review. A well that produces water may still require storage or a different building layout.

sections.heading: Use nearby records to plan your Golden lot
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then compare completed wells in the nearest part of Golden rather than averaging the entire five-mile area. Look at reported depth, test yield, static water level, permit use and aquifer description. Records from West Pleasant View, Applewood, East Pleasant View, Fairmount, Genesee and Idledale can provide context, but they do not replace a site investigation.

For an existing home, obtain the permit, well construction report, pump information, recent water test and any production test. For vacant land, have a licensed driller review access and the likely target formation before you buy or finalize plans. Also confirm DWR permit requirements and water-use limits. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be needed for some uses. Build the well, septic and driveway decisions together.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Golden, Colorado?
faq.a: Golden wells in the records have a 70-foot median depth, with the middle half from 29 to 300 feet. About 55% are under 100 feet, but the 90th percentile is 565 feet and the deepest record is 1,997 feet. Local formation, elevation and fractured-bedrock conditions can make one parcel very different from another.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Golden?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 70-foot median depth, drilling is about $3,500 to $4,900. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $9,500 to $16,900. Access, extra depth, casing, grout and site conditions can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do Golden wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 7.2-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 5.0 to 11.0 gallons per minute. About 3% report under 1 gallon per minute, while 64% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Only 503 wells report yield, so request the actual test for the property.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Golden?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that any individual well is safe to drink. Nearby mapped environmental information includes 170 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 200 historic mine features and 25 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test an existing well through a qualified laboratory and review local land-use and cleanup information before relying on it.

faq.q: Is groundwater getting deeper in Golden?
faq.a: The reported decade medians vary rather than showing a simple steady trend: 26 feet below surface in the 1960s, 92 feet in the 1980s, 21 feet in the 2010s and 120 feet in the 2020s. Only 125 wells report static water level, and locations differ, so obtain a current measurement for the specific property.
